sources.entry: Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Synchronization but Were Afraid to Ask - Measures line-transfer cost between cores by coherence state and distance, the figure behind every contention rule.

summary.title: Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Synchronization but Were Afraid to Ask
summary.one_liner: Learn how cache-coherence states, socket placement and lock design determine synchronization cost and scalability on modern many-core processors, based on measurements across four platforms.
keywords: how expensive is locking on multicore
takeaways: Crossing sockets makes any operation on a cache line 2 to 7.5 times slower than intra-socket operations, even without contention.
Loads and stores are not significantly cheaper than atomic operations, since memory fences often accompany them.
No single locking scheme wins everywhere; a well-implemented ticket lock performs best in most low-contention workloads.
Message passing helps mainly when many threads contend for a few data items; under low contention locks usually do better.
Synchronization scalability is largely determined by hardware, so keeping synchronization within one socket is preferable.
summary.summary: The paper is a broad measurement study of synchronization across hardware and software layers. The authors use their ccbench tool to measure cache-line operation latencies by MESI-style state and core placement, then test locks, message passing, a hash table, Memcached and a software transactional memory via their SSYNC suite. The platforms are a 4-socket AMD Opteron, an 8-socket Intel Xeon, a Sun Niagara 2 and a Tilera TILE-Gx36. The findings argue that scalability of synchronization is mainly a property of the hardware.
